note: Plain-language glossary. Written from IRS publications; general information only.

items.definition: Your total income minus certain adjustments, such as deductible IRA contributions, student loan interest, and half of self-employment tax. Many credits and deductions depend on it.
A separate tax calculation that limits some deductions. You pay whichever is higher: regular tax or AMT.
A corrected return (Form 1040-X for individuals) filed to fix mistakes or claim something you missed.
An IRS review of a return to check that income, deductions, and credits are reported correctly. Most are handled by mail.
Tax a payer must withhold (generally 24%) from certain payments when you haven’t given them a correct taxpayer ID.
What you paid for an asset, adjusted for improvements and depreciation. It’s used to figure your gain or loss when you sell.
Most property you own for personal use or investment, such as stocks, bonds, and your home.
The profit when you sell a capital asset for more than its basis.
The loss when you sell a capital asset for less than its basis. Losses can offset gains, and up to $3,000 a year can offset other income.
An unused loss, credit, or deduction that you can apply to a future year.
A credit for part of what you pay for care of a child under 13 or a disabled dependent so you can work or look for work.
A credit for each qualifying child under 17 who meets the relationship, residency, and Social Security number rules. Part of it may be refundable.
Income counts as received when it’s made available to you, even if you don’t actually take it yet.
For businesses that sell products: the cost of the inventory sold during the year.
An amount that reduces your tax dollar for dollar. Refundable credits can produce a refund even if you owe no tax.
An amount subtracted from income before tax is figured, which lowers taxable income.
A qualifying child or qualifying relative whom you can claim on your return if the IRS tests are met.
Deducting the cost of business or rental property over its useful life instead of all at once.
Having your refund deposited straight into a bank account. It’s the fastest way to get a refund.
Wages, salaries, tips, and net earnings from self-employment. Investment income and pensions are not earned income.
A refundable credit for workers with low to moderate income. The amount depends on income, filing status, and number of qualifying children.
Your total tax divided by your income. It’s usually much lower than your top (marginal) rate.
Filing your return electronically. It’s faster and more accurate than paper filing.
A nine-digit number the IRS assigns to businesses, employers, estates, and trusts.
A tax professional licensed by the IRS who can represent taxpayers before the IRS on any tax matter.
Tax paid during the year on income that isn’t subject to withholding, such as self-employment or investment income. Usually paid quarterly.
A tax on specific goods or activities, such as fuel or certain business activities.
An amount Ohio lets you subtract for yourself and each dependent, based on your income.
More time to file your return (usually six months). It does not give you more time to pay.
The price property would sell for between a willing buyer and a willing seller who both know the relevant facts.
Social Security and Medicare taxes withheld from wages. Employers pay a matching amount.
The category that determines your tax rates and standard deduction: single, married filing jointly, married filing separately, head of household, or qualifying surviving spouse.
A family of forms reporting income other than wages, such as contract pay, interest, dividends, and retirement distributions.
A benefit an employer provides in addition to pay, such as health insurance or a company car. Some are taxable.
The federal unemployment tax that employers pay. Employees don’t pay it.
A tax on large gifts. Most people never pay it because of the annual exclusion and the lifetime exemption.
All income you receive that isn’t specifically excluded from tax.
A filing status for unmarried people who pay more than half the cost of keeping up a home for a qualifying person.
A tax-advantaged account for medical costs, available with a high-deductible health plan.
A six-digit number from the IRS that helps stop someone else from filing a return with your Social Security number.
Someone who works for themselves rather than as an employee. They usually receive a 1099-NEC and pay self-employment tax.
A personal retirement savings account with tax advantages. Traditional and Roth IRAs are taxed differently.
A tax ID the IRS issues to people who need one but can’t get a Social Security number.
A payment plan with the IRS for paying a tax balance over time.
Specific expenses, such as mortgage interest, state and local taxes, and charitable gifts, that you can deduct instead of taking the standard deduction.
A rule that taxes some of a child’s investment income at the parent’s rate.
A legal seizure of property or money to pay a tax debt, used only after notices.
The government’s legal claim against your property when you don’t pay a tax debt.
A gain on an asset held more than one year. It’s taxed at lower rates (0%, 15%, or 20%) than ordinary income.
The rate that applies to your next dollar of income: your top bracket.
A filing status where spouses combine income and deductions on one return. Both are responsible for the tax.
A filing status where spouses file their own returns. It often results in higher tax but can make sense in some cases.
A 1.45% tax on all wages (2.9% total with the employer’s share), plus an extra 0.9% on high wages.
AGI with certain amounts added back. Different tax benefits define it differently.
An income tax charged by many Ohio cities and villages, often collected through RITA or CCA.
An extra 3.8% tax on investment income for people with income above certain thresholds.
A credit that can lower your tax to zero but can’t produce a refund by itself.
A letter from a tax agency. Read it carefully and respond by the deadline, or ask us for help.
An agreement with the IRS to settle a tax debt for less than the full amount, for people who qualify.
Income taxed at regular rates, such as wages, interest, and business income.
A business, such as a partnership or S corporation, whose income is taxed on the owners’ returns instead of the business’s.
Taxes on wages: income tax withholding, Social Security, Medicare, and unemployment taxes.
An extra charge for filing late, paying late, or understating tax. Interest is charged separately.
A form that lets an authorized representative act for you before the IRS.
The number paid tax preparers must have and include on returns they prepare.
A deduction of up to 20% of qualified business income for many owners of pass-through businesses.
Dividends that meet IRS rules and are taxed at the lower long-term capital gains rates.
A child who meets the relationship, age, residency, support, and joint-return tests for tax benefits.
A dependent who isn’t a qualifying child but meets the relationship or household, income, and support tests.
Money returned to you when you paid more tax during the year than you owe.
A credit that can produce a refund even if you owe no tax.
The minimum amount you must withdraw each year from most retirement accounts once you reach the required age.
Whether you are a full-year resident, part-year resident, or nonresident of Ohio, which affects how your income is taxed.
A retirement account funded with after-tax money. Qualified withdrawals are tax-free.
A corporation that elects to pass its income through to its shareholders’ returns.
Paying at least a set percentage of last year’s or this year’s tax during the year to avoid an underpayment penalty.
The form sole proprietors use to report business income and expenses.
An Ohio income tax charged by some school districts, filed with Form SD 100.
Social Security and Medicare tax for people who work for themselves, figured on Schedule SE.
A gain on an asset held one year or less. It’s taxed at ordinary income rates.
A 6.2% tax on wages up to the annual wage base (12.4% for the self-employed).
Someone who owns an unincorporated business alone.
A fixed deduction based on filing status that you can take instead of itemizing.
An itemized deduction for state and local income or sales taxes and property taxes, up to a yearly cap.
The time limit for the IRS to assess tax or for you to claim a refund, usually three years.
A filing status for up to two years after a spouse’s death for someone with a dependent child.
A range of income taxed at a given rate. Only the income within that range is taxed at that rate.
The 12-month period a return covers. For most people it’s the calendar year.
Income after deductions. It’s the amount your tax rates apply to.
An independent IRS office that helps taxpayers resolve problems that normal channels haven’t fixed.
Any number used to identify a taxpayer, such as an SSN, ITIN, or EIN.
A summary of your tax return or account information from the IRS.
A penalty for not paying enough tax during the year through withholding or estimated payments.
The form employers give employees showing wages and taxes withheld for the year.
The form employees give employers to set federal income tax withholding.
Tax taken out of your pay or other income and sent to the government on your behalf.
